--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.lukes_partitioning()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: >- Optimally partition a tree into clusters of bounded size (Lukes' algorithm). twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.lukes_partitioning()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: >- Optimally partition a tree into clusters of bounded size (Lukes' algorithm). title: >- [Graph.lukes_partitioning()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: >- Optimally partition a tree into clusters of bounded size (Lukes' algorithm). page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Optimally partition a tree into clusters of bounded size (Lukes' algorithm). ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L41760-L41892){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.lukes_partitioning( max_size, node_weight_attr=None, weight_attr=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Lukes partitioning](../assets/graphs/lukes-partitioning.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A path of six nodes, A to F, cut into connected clusters of at most three nodes. The best split cuts only the middle edge C to D (dashed), keeping 4 of the 5 edges inside clusters: A, B, C in the accent color and D, E, F in teal, as the card lists." width="100%"} Cuts a tree into connected clusters whose total node weight is at most `max_size`, keeping as much edge weight inside clusters as possible (equivalently, cutting the lightest possible set of edges). It solves bounded-size clustering exactly on trees, as when grouping the branches of a distribution network into service areas, packing a hierarchy into pages or memory blocks, or splitting a phylogeny into balanced clades. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [max_size]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The maximum total node weight of a cluster. [node_weight_attr]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional node attribute with non-negative integer weights (default: every node weighs 1). [weight_attr]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional edge attribute with the value of keeping an edge inside a cluster, which every edge must hold as a number; `"weight"` names the weight field. If `None` (default), each edge's weight field is used (`1` where missing, so on an unweighted graph every edge is worth 1). ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[set[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The clusters as sets of node IDs. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is not a tree, a node weight is not a non-negative integer, a single node weighs more than `max_size`, or `weight_attr=` names an attribute that an edge lacks or holds as a non-number. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Lukes (1974) is a dynamic program over the tree: for each subtree and each possible weight of the cluster containing its root, the best kept edge weight, combined child by child either by cutting the edge to the child or by merging the child's root cluster. It runs in $O(n K^2)$ time for `max_size` $K$ and finds an optimum; the kept weight matches NetworkX's `lukes_partitioning` (which may return a different optimal partition). Edge direction is ignored. ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~kernighan_lin_bisection`) : Split any graph into two halves with few edges between them. [](`~cut_size`) : The number of edges between two sets of nodes. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A path of six nodes, cut into pieces of at most three nodes, keeps four of its five edges when cut in the middle: ::: {#19d6a87c .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec path = ec.Graph.from_edges([ ("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E"), ("E", "F"), ]) label = path.get_label_from_id [sorted(label(n) for n in c) for c in path.lukes_partitioning(3)] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [['A', 'B', 'C'], ['D', 'E', 'F']] ``` ::: ::: ### Clusters of a tree A balanced binary tree has 31 nodes in five levels. A connected cluster of `k` nodes keeps `k - 1` edges, so on an unweighted tree, keeping the most edges means using the fewest clusters. With at most four nodes in a cluster (left), the tree needs nine, one more than the sizes alone would allow, since every cluster must be connected. With at most seven (right), five clusters are enough: ::: {#f348c81a .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} tree = ec.Graph().add_balanced_tree(2, 4) tree.layout_kamada_kawai() { size: sorted(len(c) for c in tree.lukes_partitioning(size)) for size in (4, 7) } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {4: [3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 4], 7: [3, 7, 7, 7, 7]} ``` ::: ::: ::: {layout-ncol="2"} ::: {#750af893 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} clusters = tree.lukes_partitioning(4) tree.set_node_attrs( "up_to_4", {n: i for i, c in enumerate(clusters) for n in c} ) tree.plot( layout="pos", color_by="up_to_4", edge_color_by="up_to_4", show_labels=False, width=320, height=360, legend=False, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
